title: Stochastic Knapsack without Relaxing the Capacity
authors: Anindya De (University of Pennsylvania, USA), Sanjeev Khanna (University of Pennsylvania, USA), Nathan White (University of Pennsylvania, USA)
abstract: We present the first polynomial-time approximation scheme (PTAS) for the stochastic knapsack problem that does not relax the knapsack's capacity. Given n items with known arbitrary independent size distributions and fixed profits, an accuracy parameter  ε ∊ (0,1), and an overflow probability bound α, our algorithm computes a set of items with profit at least (1-ε) times optimal, while ensuring the probability of exceeding the capacity is at most 4√α+ε. Prior to our work, no PTAS was known without either allowing a (1+ε) capacity expansion or restricting to special distribution classes (such as Poisson or Gaussian). A key tool in our algorithm is an anti-concentration result that allows us to handle "low-profit" items by adapting a known PTAS result for the case when we are allowed to expand knapsack capacity by a (1+ε) factor. We then show that we are able to convert this solution into another solution with a similar profit which strictly obeys the knapsack capacity, but requires that we relax the overflow probability to a 4√α+ε factor. In the special case where the item sizes are scaled Bernoulli random variables (which have support on 0 and exactly one other value), we extend our approach to obtain an improved overflow probability guarantee of α +ε. We make this improvement by exploiting the fact that these random variables are defined by only two parameters (the probability of being non-zero and the non-zero value in the support), which allows us to avoid some of the complexity and overhead of our algorithm for arbitrary distributions.

I. I NTRODUCTION
In the classical knapsack problem, the size of each item
is known deterministically, and the goal is to maximize profit
subject to the constraint that the total size of the selected items
is at most the knapsack capacity. While the problem is NPHard, there exists a simple pseudopolynomial-time dynamic
program to solve the problem exactly, and it admits a PTAS.
However, in many situations, such as network routing, the
item sizes cannot be known in advance and instead are subject
to some random process. This motivated previous works to
study the (bounded overflow1 Stochastic Knapsack Problem
(see i.e. [1]–[5]). In this problem, the size of each item is
an independent random variable, and the goal is to maximize
profit subject to the constraint that the probability of the total
size of the selected items exceeding the knapsack capacity

B. Other Related Work
Beyond knapsack, several other stochastic variants of optimization problems have been studied, including minimum
spanning tree, geometric problems and general utility functions
(see e.g. [6]–[8]). Similar to the Stochastic Knapsack Problem,
these variants usually ask for the largest profit relevant feasible
solution subject to a stochastic capacity constraint. When
relaxing the size of the constraint along with the overflow
probability, [8] gave a PTAS for a wide range of utility
functions and combinatorial problems.

IV. C ONSTRUCTING S UBPROBLEMS FOR C OMBINING S ETS
In this section, we develop a key technical tool that is used
in our main result (Algorithm 1) as well as by our improved
algorithm for Bernoulli items (Algorithm 3).
Suppose we know some set T is part of the optimal solution
(say by enumerating through all possibilities, as we do for
certain high-profit items in Algorithm 1). Is there some way we
may “recurse” on the remaining items to construct a set with
near-optimal profit and low overflow probability, compared to
the complete optimal solution? If the items had deterministic
sizes, this would be simple: reduce the original capacity by
the size of T , and recurse on the remaining items. Of course,
the stochastic nature of the items complicates this process, and
we are not able to reduce to the single stochastic constraint
in such a straightforward way. Nonetheless, in this section,
we show that with multiple simultaneous (stochastic) capacity
constraints, we are able to, in a certain sense, recurse on the
remaining items as we would for items with deterministic
sizes.
We accomplish this goal by a “coarsening” of the support of
X(T ), while increasing overflow probability by only poly(ε).
In particular, we divide the support of X(T ) into poly(1/ε)
intervals, each containing poly(ε) probability mass. Informally, then, the exact distribution within those intervals can be
ignored (up to a poly(ε) loss in probability mass), allowing
us to assume X(T ) is supported on only the endpoints of
these intervals. So, we only need a set S to satisfy poly(1/ε)
(stochastic) constraints to adequately control the probability
X(S ∪ T ) ≥ 1. This process and its guarantees are formalized
in Lemma IV.4.
In more detail, the guarantees of Lemma IV.4 can be thought
of as follows. Consider disjoint sets of items A, B and a given
T ⊆ B. Suppose there is some unknown S ∈ A (i.e. some
optimal solution) and we want to construct a set S ′ ⊆ A so that
the overflow probability of S ′ ∪ T is not too much larger than
that of S ∪ T while S ′ and S have comparable profit. Lemma
IV.4 shows that there exists a set C of poly(1/ε) capacity
constraints such that any set S ′ which (approximately) respects
C has the property that S ′ ∪ T does not have too much larger
overflow probability than S ∪ T . Moreover, S itself respects
C, so the highest profit subset of A which respects C has at
least as much profit as S.
If we knew this set of constraints C, (approximately) solving
the multi-constraint stochastic knapsack over A with constraints C would produce a desired S ′ (this is exactly what we
use Algorithm 2 for in Algorithm 1). Fortunately, Lemma IV.1,
along with Lemma IV.4, shows that, given T , there can only
be 2poly(1/ε) options for C, and so we may simply enumerate

At a high level, Algorithm 2 has three major phases:
1) Pre-processing which removes a small fraction of items
and then groups the remaining items using a scheme
similar to that of [3].
2) Enumeration through various statistics about a solution,
per group, to match those of an optimal solution. Then,
finding a set of items from each group which approximately match the given group statistics.
3) Post-processing to ensure low overflow probability. The
approximate nature of the prior enumeration introduces
some error, which we correct for by removing a small
fraction of items from each constructed set.
a) Pre-processing (Lines 1 - 14): The algorithm begins
by removing some types of items which are challenging to
handle in Lines 2 through 4; we note that Line 3 is the only
place where we use randomness in the algorithm. We can
then group the items using our analog of the grouping of [3]
(Theorem VI.16) and create the guesses of group statistics we
will match in the next step.
b) Enumeration (Lines 15 - 30): For each enumerated
setting of each group’s statistics (which correspond to things
like the mean, expected number of large realizations, and
so on), we first compute the relevant value for each item.
Fortunately, the statistics are all linear (since they can all be
described as an expectation). So, for each group, we are able
to select which items from the group to include by solving
a (deterministic) multi-dimensional knapsack problem, where
the constraints correspond to the given statistics.
c) Post-processing (Lines 31 - 36): Since we are only
guaranteed to have approximately matched the statistics of an
optimal solution in the prior enumeration, for our analysis to
go through we need to remove some items to correct for this
error. Fortunately, since all the items are low profit, like the
pre-processing steps, this can be done while only reducing the
profit to a 1 − poly(ε) factor of the original. The outputted
collection is then simply the collection of all sets constructed
across the enumeration of statistics.

Let C = {(tj , αj )}j∈[γ] be the capacity constraints, and let
t1 be the smallest threshold in C. Call any item likely-large

For each j ∈ [γ], we sample a threshold θj uniformly at random from [ε9 tj , 2ε9 tj ], and discard any items with too much
